stories.headline: Trump border crackdown has crossings at historic lows; former chief has warning
stories.note: DHS says FY2026 southwest border apprehensions hit 98,708 — about 95% below Biden-era averages — with a full fiscal year of zero migrant releases.
body: DHS reported Thursday that Border Patrol logged just 98,708 southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026 — roughly 95% below the Biden-era annual average of more than 1.8 million — and finished a full fiscal year with zero migrant releases into the country.

That works out to about 270 apprehensions a day, versus roughly 5,000 under DHS's Biden-era average. September marked the 17th straight month without Border Patrol releases. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Trump promised a secure border "and the data proves he delivered."

Retired Yuma Sector Border Patrol Chief Chris Clem told Fox the contrast with December 2021 is stark, when daily arrivals in his sector jumped from about 25 a year earlier to more than 1,000 — and agents were "outnumbered, literally 100 to one."

Clem credits tougher enforcement and ending catch-and-release for killing smugglers' old pitch that migrants would be processed and let go. Border czar Tom Homan separately said ICE hit its highest single-day deportation total since Trump returned and its busiest removal month in September.

Why it matters: These numbers are a signature Trump deliverable heading into the midterms — and Clem warned a Congress eager to reverse the president could jam up funding and policy if Democrats gain ground.

stories.headline: Dems' affordability crusade collides with eye-popping price tag for socialist immigration plans
stories.note: A White House CEA report pegs DSA-backed mass amnesty and benefits at $440B–$613B over a decade, undercutting Democrats' midterm affordability message.
body: A White House Council of Economic Advisers report, first obtained by Fox, estimates that DSA-backed mass amnesty and expanded federal benefits for illegal immigrants could cost taxpayers $440 billion to $613 billion over the next decade.

The council puts the average lifetime net fiscal cost of an illegal immigrant at $166,716 — more than the roughly $124,000 College Board figures for four years at an average in-state public university. Under its model, the current illegal immigrant population accounts for $1.4 trillion to $1.9 trillion in taxpayer costs.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said Trump "supercharged ICE to remove criminal illegal aliens," while "radical Democrats want to go back to their extreme open border policies and grant amnesty" that would make America less safe and cost taxpayers billions.

The report also warns that ending Trump-backed enforcement would erase $227 billion to $287 billion in projected savings. Expanded SNAP, housing aid, and Medicaid eligibility alone could add $361 billion to $475 billion over ten years. Broader DSA agenda costs are pegged at about $49 trillion, or roughly $355,000 per household.
Why it matters: Democrats are running on affordability; the White House is tying socialist immigration plans to higher costs and weaker borders — a midterm contrast Republicans can hammer.

stories.headline: Democrat's debate 'cue cards' steal spotlight in high-stakes Senate clash
stories.note: Alaska Dem Mary Peltola got hammered after appearing to read from cue cards in her debate with GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, who quipped she can't cue-card her way through the Senate.
body: Alaska Democratic Senate hopeful Mary Peltola drew fierce GOP mockery Thursday after she appeared to read from notecards during her debate with Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in a race Cook rates a toss-up.

Sullivan posted afterward: "Really, Mary? Reading off a script? You can't cue-card your way through the Senate." On stage he asked moderators whether candidates got questions in advance; they said no, and he replied he was "just watching my opponent." Peltola said she was better "prepared."

NRSC official Joanna Rodriguez jabbed that Peltola seemed unable to "string a sentence together without reading from the talking points" her "Lower 48 handlers" wrote. The RNC research arm noted she appeared to need a script even on Alaska's fishing industry.

The debate also got personal when Sullivan cited New York Times reporting and claimed 25 of her staff quit amid mistreatment allegations; Peltola called those claims fabrications or exaggerations. They also sparred over Alaska's LNG pipeline and foreign investment commitments.
Why it matters: Republicans are defending a narrow Senate majority, and a viral stumble by a top Democratic pickup hope in a Trump-won state is free ammunition for Sullivan and the NRSC.

stories.headline: Kash Patel demands MS NOW apologize after network's false report claiming FBI director visited Russia
stories.note: FBI Director Kash Patel says MS NOW falsely claimed he landed in Russia when he was in Virginia — and wants apologies to the FBI, law enforcement, and the public.
body: FBI Director Kash Patel is demanding more than a correction after MS NOW falsely reported Wednesday that he had "landed in Russia" for meetings, citing two anonymous FBI sources and floating agency concern about a Kremlin visit.

Patel was actually in Virginia honoring law enforcement at Liberty University. The FBI's Rapid Response account mocked the report in real time. Correspondent Ken Dilanian later corrected on air, saying Patel "did not, in fact, land in Russia today and remains in the U.S."

Patel wrote that the network put him in Russia on anonymous sources, called it a "basic verification failure," and said three apologies are owed: "to this FBI, to the law enforcement community, and to the American People." MS NOW pointed to its on-air correction.

Fox reported speculation that the false tip may have helped expose leakers; an FBI official neither confirmed nor denied a sting but said the two leakers would "likely" be identified and that the bureau is "always hunting leakers."

Why it matters: A major liberal network airing a false Russia scare about Trump's FBI director — then walking it back — hands Republicans another media-credibility and leaker story before the midterms.

stories.headline: Illegal alien busted allegedly hauling enough fentanyl to potentially kill state’s entire population — twice
stories.note: Nevada cops stopped a speeding pickup and say they found hundreds of pounds of fentanyl and meth — another reminder why Trump's border and interior enforcement matter.
body: Federal prosecutors say illegal immigrant Francisco Joel Garcia Farias, 26, was stopped for speeding on U.S. 93 near Ash Springs, Nevada, on Oct. 13 — and deputies with a narcotics dog found 13 totes packed with roughly 30 pounds of suspected fentanyl and 677 pounds of suspected meth.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Sigal Chattah said the roughly 14 kilograms of fentanyl alone is about seven million potentially lethal 2-milligram doses — enough to kill more than twice Nevada's population — with the combined haul valued around $2 million on the street.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said anyone who plans to put deadly fentanyl on American streets will be prosecuted, and credited federal and local partners for keeping the drugs off the street. HSI and the Lincoln County Sheriff's Office worked the case.

Garcia Farias faces possession-with-intent charges for 400 grams or more of a fentanyl mixture and 500 grams or more of meth. Each count carries a 10-year mandatory minimum and up to life if he is convicted.
Why it matters: DOJ itself flagged the suspect as an illegal immigrant — a concrete example Republicans can cite for why Trump's border and interior enforcement fight fentanyl and cartel trafficking.

stories.headline: Fears of China spying on US military prompt GOP hawks to demand retaliation against the shipping giant
stories.note: House Republicans want DHS to strip CCP-owned COSCO of U.S. port privileges after reports its ships used gear to intercept U.S. military communications.
body: Three top House Republicans — China Committee Chair John Moolenaar, Intelligence Chair Rick Crawford, and Rep. Carlos Gimenez — wrote DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Oct. 14 demanding CCP-owned shipping giant COSCO lose its Coast Guard Qualship 21 port privileges.

As of mid-July, 11 COSCO vessels were still in the program that cuts routine U.S. port inspections for trusted operators, even though the Pentagon put COSCO on its Chinese military company list in January 2025. September reporting alleged COSCO ships used concealed gear to intercept U.S. military communications near American coasts.

COSCO denied the spying claims and said its gear is for commercial navigation. The Coast Guard told Fox that on Oct. 15 the commandant ordered an immediate review of COSCO's Qualship participation and noted stronger eligibility rules added in January for national-security concerns.

The lawmakers want enrollments revoked, renewals refused, more scrutiny of CCP-tied shippers, and answers on whether intelligence warnings were ignored after the Pentagon designation. They also floated removing Hong Kong from the Coast Guard's qualified flag list.

Why it matters: GOP hawks are forcing DHS to choose between convenience for a CCP shipping giant and hardening ports against alleged military intelligence collection — a national-security contrast with softer China policies.

stories.headline: Trump administration sues California over 20,000 suspected noncitizens on state’s voter rolls
stories.note: After California blew off DOJ's 48-hour demand, Trump's DOJ sued to keep alleged noncitizen ballots from diluting citizen votes in the midterms.
body: Two days after DOJ gave California 48 hours to review a federal list of more than 20,000 suspected noncitizens on the state's voter rolls, the Trump administration sued Thursday, arguing the state refused to cooperate and risked letting noncitizens dilute citizen votes in the midterms.

LA's top federal prosecutor Bill Essayli said California officials "were given an opportunity to remove noncitizens from their voter rolls and to sequester ballots returned from suspected ineligible voters. They refused," and that DOJ is going to court "to demand that the votes of American citizens not be diluted by noncitizens."

Federal officials had supplied Los Angeles County a password-protected drive naming suspected noncitizens who allegedly got mail-in ballots. County Clerk Dean Logan said he received the drive but did not consider it secure and had not yet accessed the files while consulting state lawyers.

Gov. Gavin Newsom called the suit a "desperate attempt" at voter suppression just weeks before Election Day and said courts have limited the federal role in state election processes. DOJ said only citizens may vote in federal elections and that immediate action is needed.

Why it matters: After California blew off the 48-hour warning, Trump's DOJ escalated to court — putting Newsom's election practices on trial before Nov. 3 and spotlighting noncitizen voting enforcement.
